title: The Builders of the Wall
summary: The chapter records who rebuilt each section of Jerusalem's wall and gates, moving around the city counterclockwise from the Sheep Gate and back again. Priests, Levites, temple servants, district rulers, townsmen from across Judah, goldsmiths, perfumers, merchants, and one man with his daughters all take part, many working opposite their own homes. Only the nobles of Tekoa are singled out for refusing to put their shoulders to the work.
story: Chapter 2 ended with the people saying let us start rebuilding and the opponents mocking them. Chapter 3 shows the building itself, not as a story but as a record. It pauses the action to name the people who did the work, before chapter 4 returns to the mounting opposition and chapter 6 records the wall's completion in fifty-two days. Placed here, the list shows that the wall was not Nehemiah's achievement alone but the work of the whole community, organized section by section. It is also a snapshot of who lived in and around Jerusalem in 445 BC, many of whom appear again in the book's later lists and events.
historical:
The chapter describes a circuit of the wall as it stood in Nehemiah's day, starting at the Sheep Gate near the temple on the north and moving west, south, and up the eastern side before returning to the Sheep Gate (verse 32). Most scholars think Nehemiah's Jerusalem was much smaller than the city before 587 or 586 BC, covering the temple mount and the narrow ridge of the old City of David, rather than the broader western hill that had been enclosed in the late monarchy. The Broad Wall in verse 8 may be connected with a massive late eighth century BC wall uncovered by the archaeologist Nahman Avigad in the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem in the 1970s, which he named after this verse; whether Nehemiah's builders used that line is debated.

The list mentions rulers of districts and half-districts (Jerusalem, Beth-haccherem, Mizpah, Beth-zur, Keilah), which gives a glimpse of the Persian administration of the province of Judah. Some workers came from towns outside the province proper, such as Jericho, Gibeon, and Tekoa. Several names connect with other parts of Ezra-Nehemiah: Eliashib the high priest was a grandson of Jeshua (Nehemiah 12:10), Meremoth son of Uriah had received Ezra's treasure (Ezra 8:33), and Meshullam son of Berechiah would later give his daughter in marriage to Tobiah's son (Nehemiah 6:18). The Nehemiah son of Azbuk in verse 16 is a different man from the governor.
cultural:
Ancient city walls had gates that were more than openings: they were towers with heavy wooden doors, bolts, and bars, and they served as markets and courts. Several gates here are named for what passed through them or what was nearby. The Sheep Gate, near the temple, was probably where animals for sacrifice were brought in; the Fish Gate may have been where fish from the coast or the Sea of Galilee were sold; the Dung Gate led to the city's refuse dump; the Fountain Gate stood near a spring or pool; and the Water Gate probably opened toward the Gihon spring.

The list shows how work was organized in a small society. Priests built near the temple, often in front of their own houses (verses 1, 28). Families and guilds (goldsmiths, perfumers, merchants) took sections, and people from outlying towns sent work parties. Assigning sections by household meant that people defended what was closest to them, a practical arrangement that also gave each family a stake in the whole. The mention of Shallum working with his daughters (verse 12) is unusual in an ancient building list and suggests he had no sons, or that the daughters' labor was notable enough to record. The refusal of the Tekoite nobles, who would not bend their necks to the work, reflects a social elite unwilling to do manual labor or to submit to Nehemiah's supervisors.
literary: The chapter is a structured list, repeating a small set of formulas: next to him, made repairs, repaired another section, installed its doors, bolts, and bars. The verb to repair (literally to strengthen) appears again and again, giving the chapter a steady, working rhythm. The circuit begins and ends at the Sheep Gate with priests and goldsmiths, forming a closed loop that mirrors the wall itself. The first half (verses 1-15) is organized mainly around gates, while the second half (verses 16-32), along the eastern side, is organized around houses, towers, and landmarks. Only one negative note interrupts the list, the Tekoite nobles in verse 5, and the same Tekoites are shown in verse 27 repairing a second section. The chapter has no dialogue and no narrative drama, yet its detail makes it one of the most concrete pictures of a biblical community at work.

outline.t: The north wall: the Sheep Gate and the Fish Gate
The northwest: the Jeshanah Gate to the Broad Wall
The Valley Gate and the Dung Gate
The southeast: the Fountain Gate and the City of David
The east: the Horse Gate back to the Sheep Gate

doctrines.note: The wall is rebuilt by the whole people, each group at its own section: priests and merchants, rulers and craftsmen, townsmen and daughters. The chapter pictures the community of God as a body where many members share one work.

The priests consecrate the Sheep Gate and the wall they build (verse 1). The city's defenses are dedicated to God, reflecting the conviction that Jerusalem as a whole, not only the temple, belonged to the LORD.

The work of restoration is shared by people of every rank and occupation. God's purposes advance not only through leaders but through ordinary people taking responsibility for the section in front of them.

words.note: Chazaq, to be strong or strengthen, here meaning to repair, used about thirty-five times in the chapter. The same verb described the people strengthening their hands for the work in 2:18. Its repetition gives the chapter a double sense: as the wall is made strong, so are the people.

Qadash, to consecrate or set apart as holy. Eliashib and the priests consecrated the Sheep Gate and the wall (verse 1). This act anticipates the great dedication of the finished wall in 12:27-43 and marks the rebuilding as sacred work, not merely civil engineering.

Yad, hand. The phrase translated next to them is literally at their hand, and it recurs throughout the chapter. The image is of workers standing side by side, each at the hand of the next, joined along the whole length of the wall.

Bat, daughter. Shallum repaired his section with the help of his daughters (verse 12). Ancient building records rarely mention women as laborers, and the note stands out. Whatever the reason, the chapter records their work by name alongside that of rulers and priests.

christ: A long list of builders, each repairing a section next to another, has no direct prophecy of Christ in it, but it anticipates the way the New Testament describes the people of God. Paul speaks of believers as members of one body, each with a part to play (1 Corinthians 12:12-27), and Peter describes them as living stones being built into a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5). The high priest begins the work at the Sheep Gate, where animals for sacrifice likely entered; John's Gospel mentions a pool by the Sheep Gate in Jesus' day (John 5:2), and the New Testament presents Jesus as both the true high priest and the Lamb of God. These connections are thematic and should not be pressed into allegory, but they show how the chapter's picture of a restored community fits the larger story.
questions: Many worked on the section of wall in front of their own homes. What is the section in front of you, the place where your faithfulness matters most directly?
Goldsmiths, perfumers, priests, and a man with his daughters all built the same wall. What does this suggest about who belongs in God's work?
The Tekoite nobles refused to put their shoulders to the work, while ordinary Tekoites repaired two sections. What keeps people with position or status from doing humble work?
